quote: which she does not experience as anything happening
why: the clause after the comma tells the reader how to take "gets big" instead of stating the fact and stopping, the trailing-explanatory-clause automatic fail.
suggestion: Cut the clause and end on the fact: "Chloe's blog gets big in about fourteen months."

quote: and then people start noticing that her summary is the length of a normal article and contains more, and by the following spring she has a readership and an inbox.
why: three unequal beats (people noticing, the summary containing more, her gaining a readership) are coordinated with "and" instead of subordinated, so nothing in the chain outranks anything else.
suggestion: "once people notice her summary runs longer than a normal article and holds more in it, she has, by the following spring, a readership and an inbox."

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
why: routes the reader's access to the credential-conversation pattern through a perception-filter verb instead of rendering the pattern itself.
suggestion: "The pattern repeats: same question, same drop-off."

quote: files it under people being funny about credentials
why: hands the abstract interpretation ("it" = the pattern) a physical storage verb, as though a read on people's behavior were a document that can be filed.
suggestion: "she decides it's people being funny about credentials, and leaves it there."

quote: and she comes out and gets a coffee and doesn't think about it again until the result arrives
why: three trivial actions (coming out, getting coffee, not thinking about it) are strung together with "and" as a default habit, giving them equal grammatical weight.
suggestion: "She comes out, gets a coffee, and stops thinking about it until the result arrives." or subordinate: "before getting a coffee on her way out, done thinking about it until the result arrives."

quote: She does not read the result as information about herself.
why: a not-X-but-Y construction in narration that denies a reading nobody in the scene asserted before restating it positively in the next sentence.
suggestion: Cut the denial and open on the positive: "She reads it as having sat an exam."

why: the clause after the comma explains how to take "doesn't pretend the questions are casual" instead of letting the detail stand on its own.
suggestion: Cut the clause: "He's thorough and he doesn't pretend the questions are casual."

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
why: part of a nine-line exchange (lines 219-249) carrying only three attribution tags total, so this turn has no tag and no action beat to mark the speaker change.
suggestion: "Asked by whom," Whitaker says, not looking up.

rule_name: Talking Heads, Anchor Dialogue in Physical Space
why: this line sits in the middle of a five-turn run (219-231) with no physical detail anywhere in it, well past the every-three-or-four-lines anchor the rule calls for, so the interrogation room has no bodies in it.
suggestion: "Whitaker sets his pen down. \"The lead researcher.\""

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
why: another untagged turn in the same long exchange, forcing the reader to count lines back to the last tag to confirm this is Whitaker.
suggestion: "And you agreed to that," he says, flat.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
why: "for a while" is named directly in the rule as a universal duration marker used regardless of what kind of moment is being timed, and it does no more work here than in the banned example.
suggestion: "Whitaker fills half a page before he looks up."

rule_name: Paragraph Breaks, Keep One Beat in One Paragraph
why: Whitaker's action and the dialogue it leads into (line 237) are split across a paragraph break with no shift in time, place, or speaker to justify the break.
suggestion: Merge: "Whitaker writes for a while. 'Anything else in that category?'"

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
why: untagged turn following an action beat by the same speaker, six lines past the last actual dialogue tag at line 219, so the reader has to track the alternation rather than read an attribution.
suggestion: Whitaker taps the pen twice. "Anything else in that category?"

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
quote: Would you tell me if I said it was necessary?
why: untagged turn in the same long exchange; the only tags across eleven turns are at lines 219, 240, and 249, so this line depends entirely on the reader's count.
suggestion: "Would you tell me if I said it was necessary?" he asks.

why: states the fact that she thought rather than rendering the thought itself, a summary of cognition standing in for an instance of it.
suggestion: "Talk to her first, or don't. Chloe holds the two against each other."

rule_name: Paragraph Breaks, Keep One Beat in One Paragraph
quote: Chloe thinks about it properly, which takes her a few seconds.
why: Chloe's thinking beat and her own next line of dialogue (line 249) are split into separate paragraphs though nothing shifts in time, place, or speaker between them.
suggestion: Merge into one paragraph ending on: "'I'd want to talk to her first,' she says."

quote: He asks who the school's principal donor is and she says she has no idea, that nobody there ever discussed it, that she was seven when she arrived and it never occurred to her to ask who paid for a school any more than it occurs to a child to ask who pays for a park.
why: the question, the answer, and the justifying comparison are all coordinated with "and" instead of subordinated, so the sentence cannot distinguish the trivial link from the load-bearing one.
suggestion: "He asks who the school's principal donor is; she has no idea, because nobody there ever discussed it and because she was seven when she arrived, no more likely to ask who paid for a school than a child asks who pays for a park."

rule_name: Telling After Showing, Don't Explain the Image You Just Rendered
quote: She can hear how that sounds while she's saying it.
why: narrates Chloe's awareness of how her funding answer lands immediately after the scene already showed that same effect through the answer itself, explaining the image the previous paragraph just rendered.
suggestion: Cut it and move straight to the next beat: "She says it anyway. It's true."
